video.title: How Scap Retraction Powers the One-Handed Backhand

classification.reason: The coach explains the biomechanics of scapular retraction, pull slot positioning, wrist stabilization, and grip mechanics for the one-handed backhand.

problem.title_as_question: How does scapular retraction power the one-handed backhand?
problem.definition: Players struggle to hit a powerful, fault-tolerant one-handed backhand because they fail to drive the stroke with upper back scapular retraction from an optimal forward pull slot, let the wrist collapse through contact, or use an incorrect grip angle.
problem.target_player: One-handed backhand players seeking to generate power, control, and fault tolerance through contact.

symptoms.description: The torso rotates farther than intended, resulting in shanking the ball.
The wrist breaks open or twists drastically (up to 100 degrees) right through the hitting zone, causing the string angle to change.
The player feels inability to generate force from the upper back, being forced to pull with weak arm muscles (triceps, deltoids) and risking injury.
The pulling motion travels sideways across the body instead of driving back-to-front toward the target.

causes.statement: The wrist is allowed to break freely through contact instead of using forearm tension to restrict rotation to a plane that keeps string angle stable.
Holding the racket with knuckles slanted offside at a ~135 degree volley angle rather than a strict 90-degree orthogonal angle between forearm and handle.
Catching the ball too late with the pull slot set too close to the stomach rather than out in front.
Initiating the stroke solely with one hand instead of executing a two-handed forward movement into the pull slot.
Failing to drive the racket forward using upper back scapular retraction (rhomboids and traps pulling shoulder blades together).

angles.summary: Scapular retraction powered by the rhomboids and trapezius pulling shoulder blades together is the core contact motion driving the one-handed backhand back-to-front.
Testing isometric pull against a wall or in the slot helps players feel whether upper back muscles can generate force from that contact position.
Unlike the forehand where wrist break happens harmlessly after contact, allowing the backhand wrist to break naturally causes a 100-degree angle change directly inside the hitting zone.
While a continental volley grip uses a 135-degree slanted angle, backhand groundstrokes strictly require an orthogonal 90-degree angle between forearm and handle to prevent wrist collapse.
The upper back pulling motion on the backhand engages the same powerful musculature trained through weighted pull-ups or rowing exercises.

solutions.summary: Position the racket against a wall at estimated contact spots and test pulling to locate the exact pull slot where upper back muscles generate maximal force.
solutions.external_goal: Push or pull against a wall to test force generation.

solutions.summary: Prepare with racket head pointed down, advance into the pull slot, and execute a firm block swing keeping the wrist angle locked, only adding looser preparation and racket rotation once contact control is mastered.
solutions.external_goal: Keep racket head down and maintain fixed wrist angle into the pull slot.

solutions.summary: Initiate the forward movement toward the pull slot with two hands on the racket, only separating the off-hand right before the upper back pull.
Verify that the racket handle forms a strict 90-degree orthogonal right angle with the forearm and knuckles remain parallel to the handle rather than slanted.
solutions.external_goal: Maintain a 90-degree right angle between the forearm and handle.
